title: TOUJOURS PLUS VERS L’OUEST, MARCHE TOURMENTÉE D’UNE FAMILLE VERS LA LIBERTÉ  (1914-1919)
description: ALWAYS MORE TOWARDS THE WEST A FAMILY'S TORMENTED MARCH TOWARDS FREEDOM (1914-1919) It was on a cheerful summer afternoon. The sun bathed the large villa of the "Conifers" and reflected on its high white and black Norman-style gables which had in vain claimed to give the house the air of a rustic cottage. The family was dispersed in the park where we heard joyful cries. The father, preoccupied with collecting original documents on the language of children, discreetly listened in a corner of the groves to the stammerings of his youngest daughter Irene, whose childish vocabulary he tried to build up. Admittedly, this peace was not without a little anxiety, just as the blue of this July sky was already strewn towards the west with padded cumuli, the whiteness of which passed gently towards the bluish-gray announcing the showers. Visitors - there were many of them at the "Conifers" whose Wednesday tennis was very popular - had spoken of the Serajvo attack and the international tension that resulted from it. But, how many times had the world not been alerted by differences between nations, without harm ensuing! Fashoda and Agadir were fresh in our memories and after all our French mother, from our earliest childhood, while talking to us about the war of 1870, had she not made us understand that "the German machine guns had become so terrible that the we would never again think of giving them the opportunity to function”. Moreover, hadn't William II, the previous year, invited the peoples of the world to unite fraternally for a lasting peace? Despite the fragility of human happiness, aren't we too willing to believe what we hope for? Even when the ultimatums had been issued and the mobilizations started on all sides, was Belgian neutrality not sacred and would it not be respected as in 1870? In vain were people hastily returning from Germany warning us that an uninterrupted series of military trains coming from the Rurh were heading towards us, we could not believe in the felony of the "rag of paper", nor in the - saying crazy strategic imprudence to alienate one more adversary, at the time when this one came under the impulse of the Count of Broqueville, to modernize his army. Without any special fears, therefore, we had my wife and I embarked on an excursion to the coast and it was at Oost-Duinkerke that we had learned that the conflict was becoming inevitable between France and Germany. However, the customs officer, the weapon on the shoulder, next to the Belgian flag hoisted on a high dune, had appeared to us as the symbol of the inviolability of our territory. On the way back by a train full of Germans fleeing our regions with a worried air, we were disappointed not to be greeted by our driver; it had been requisitioned at the same time as the car. Returning to the home on the Chaussée de Tirlemont, we soon saw thousands of Belgian soldiers pass by, whose dress and number naively persuaded us that they would make any invader hesitate, tempted to cross our borders. Alas! Like a thunderbolt in a serene sky, we were soon astounded by the news that the Germans had committed the "unbelievable imprudence" of entering the lands of Herve. But there had been the forts sz Idège and there could be no question of seeing the Germanic legions penetrate as far as Brabant. Apart from concerns about Robert Silvercruys, my brother-in-law, then serving in the infantry around Liège, the beginning of this eminently disturbing period was still accepted with a certain smile. The German "Taubes" in the sky amused us, the temporary encampments of the guides in amaranth trousers and the sky-blue lancers around our park were an appreciable distraction. The sight of a few soldiers slumped on our embankments following forced marches suggested to us the idea of having the neighboring school transformed into a small hospital. We ourselves filled our garage with mattresses so as to be able to lodge easily the passing troops, going towards the east. One day, however, the direction of the armies was clearly in the opposite direction and we had to lodge about twenty officers. At first it was an occasion for animated and almost joyful conversations, but this atmosphere changed completely when we saw coming from Korbeek-Lo, in rich uniform, riding gravely towards the west. We could no longer doubt that the King was abandoning his stay with the Baron de Dieudonné. Civil guards had meanwhile come to occupy our park and were preparing barricades with the palms and orange trees of our greenhouses. We regaled them with a champagne which they happily accepted, telling us that after all it was better for them to be the ones to benefit than this invader whom we were seriously beginning to expect, despite the bulletins en victory from Halen and other places. which our newspapers were talking about. They had even just published an "official" statement certifying that our army had the situation well in hand and that any further penetration by the enemy was "definitely ruled out." Here again we have accepted this lie with the ease of believing in what we love that we had pointed out above. But dusty and busy troops were increasingly encumbering the chaussée de Tirlemont and one of our host officers came to warn us, looking serious, that we could not stay in our house and our park, intended to serve as a last ambush for the enemy. when the German scouts would appear on the Mol hill. Thereupon, a fatal disarray arose among us, owing to the difficulty of deciding my wife to leave what she considered to be her post of honour. Hastily they hid a few objects while leaving in the building many precious things that it would have been easy to take away. Only a few silverware had been buried underground and we left with a small trunk placed on the cart, carrying our youngest child. Were we not convinced that we would return soon after a short stay in Louvain-Ville, with our mother? The idea of fires or massacres did not even cross our minds. Hadn't the Germans generally behaved well in 1870? After a night spent in town, we awoke to the hoarse sound of cannons firing incessantly from the top of the hills of Hageland. I remembered then that, in the haste of our departure from the villa, I had forgotten to hide my shotgun. However, there were already reports of German abuses against those who possessed weapons. On my bike, I returned to the "Conifers" and while I was looking for a hiding place for the rifle, I saw a squad of dismounted Belgian spearmen arriving who were taking up position at our house. It was time to return to Louvain. The officers who saw me on my bicycle even thought I was coming from further away and asked me in vain for information on the enemy's march. Returning to my family, I learned that they were going to evacuate the rue des Joyeuses Entrees (oh irony) through which the Germans would enter and where we had taken refuge. If we couldn't stay in this house, we might as well go further to the capital where we might protect ourselves and, in any case, where we would be lost in a vast population and welcomed by our parents-in-law. This time, the decision was quickly taken and we could still catch the last train leaving Leuven for Brussels. We piled into it after talking with our cousin, the engineer Verdeyen, who, with a heavy heart, was destroying the system of tracks and signals at Louvain station, recently electrified with great skill. It was our first step towards this west which was to draw us ever further to the Pacific. The arrival in Brussels where we found a roof in the house of our Verdeyen cousins, then staying at the sea, began with a certain relief. But, it was only short-lived. The next day the Prussian cavalry was already crossing the capital, arousing more curiosity than spite among the resigned crowds who watched it march past. No applause, of course, except, alas! from our silly Dutch servants. Unaware of the speed of the enemy's advance, we thought for a moment of heading for the coast. We got on a train which, in fact, set off in the direction of Tournai, but at Ruisbroeck it stopped for a long time and ended up turning back towards Brussels. The uhlans had already cut the way. Forced therefore to establish ourselves in Brussels, we accepted the idea of making a prolonged stay there while waiting for some unknown event. The atmosphere in the capital, at first full of resignation, gradually darkened. The press releases posted in three languages by the occupier spoke only of Allied defeats. These texts had even succeeded in drowning the news of the Battle of the Marne under a cloud of small engagements, where one did not find oneself and which, naturally, were presented as "conforming to the German plan". Only the moans of a German lady about her army in danger in France gave us the impression that communiqués could hide setbacks. More and more, we felt under an embrace. The goosesteps of the soldiers, their brutal blows with their rifle butts on our cobblestones strongly crushed our hopes while the refrain of the horns of their cars was felt as an irony. But our feelings towards the invader were soon to take on an even more hostile character. During one of those walks through the streets of Brussels imposed on us by our idleness and our thirst for news, near the Louise gate, my attention was attracted by a convoy of German trucks and guns on which I was surprised see, with a lamentable air, a series of ecclesiastical professors and in particular Mgr de Becker, president of the American college. Incomprehensible at first, this intriguing spectacle was gradually completed by frightening stories from countless Louvanist refugees whom we met at every step, Louvain had been burned, many people had been killed there and especially the priests and religious, as hostages. America being still neutral at this time, it was to the Embassy of the United States that we ran for information. Unfortunately, we were received there by a somewhat grumpy Belgian who had been instructed to reply laconically to the innumerable curious people who went to this address. With a tragic air, this man affirmed that the Louvanists had really fired and that rifle shots had greeted the car of an American attaché who had gone to the scene. It all seemed not only appalling but implausible. So the investigation was continued. The most numerous testimonies were collected from people belonging to the most diverse classes. No one had seen a Louvanist, gun in hand. Gunshots had been heard in some corners of the city but - as we later learned with more certainty - they came from German soldiers. It was the latter too who had wanted to impress the Americans with anonymous gunshots. But what happened to our houses in this general sacking, which, as we had just learned, had been particularly severe at the Chaussée de Tirlemont? Above, the data were far from concordant and one could get an idea of the difficulty there is in providing details by testimony. From the top of the Lo hills, someone had seen that villas no longer had roofs, but which villas and what degree of destruction? It was also said that in the Rue des Joyeuses Entrees, my mother's house had been burned down. (We later learned that it was the house next door, set on fire because a dead horse had been picked up opposite.) Les Halles, alas! had indeed been consumed with the treasures of the old university and the incunabula of the Leuven printers of the 15th century. Appalled by this destruction of what I loved so much, I remember saying at the time that I would have given my life to save these precious relics, the glory of our institution. Needless to insist on this horrible destruction of Louvain, which belongs to history like that of Dinant and other towns. Deprived of newspapers and not yet familiar with the radio, we threw ourselves on the only newspaper that the Germans had allowed to appear. He spoke of the death of Pius X and gave the photograph of the cities where the destruction had taken place but naturally without trace of the latter. This absence of means of information revealed not only the fragility of testimonies but the ease with which legends were able to be born before the existence of the press. The fabulous arrival of Russian troops in Flanders is the best example of this. We now know that the starting point of this noise is simply the fact that among the Belgian troops had landed in Zeebrugge, there was an officer wearing a fur kepi who had surprised some spectators there. "They look like Russians!" » and repeated from mouth to mouth this reflection became « Russians are coming! ". This news came naturally at the right time in an environment where one was ready to attach oneself/to any reason to hope for deliverance. This, in fact, seemed less improbable since the German troops had been seen descending in disorder on the Boulevard Léopold II, fleeing before the advance of the Belgian troops who, coming from Antwerp, had attacked them at the moment where a decisive game was being played out in France. We made every effort to obtain confirmations. Not having yet entered parliamentary circles, I had the naivety to believe that one must be well informed and I addressed myself to an important senator who affirmed to me that the news was serious. We see that if the war reveals unsuspected funds of heroism in some, it strips many personalities of the prestige which surrounds them in time of peace. Didn't a similar impression seize us when, in 1940, the French and Belgian governors, stranded in a rout in Bordeaux, appeared to us so disconcerted in their attitudes and their remarks. If in the middle of the twentieth century, legends can thus be created, and that of the Russian troops is by far not the only one which obtained credence in occupied Belgium, how can one not understand that 20 years after Waterloo, there was already a sort of Napoleonic epic? How much easier still must have been the genesis and propagation of legends in times when the marvelous was readily accepted in human facts! Will the claim that civilians fired at Leuven ever be completely eradicated from the history books - especially in Germany - and will historians of the future not consider as a prime source the unfair manner in which Churchill spoke of the role of the Belgians in Flanders at the start of the Second World War? But, ruthlessly hammering all our false hopes, the big German cannon kept firing its discharges at Maubeuge, at a rhythm as regular as the jet of geysers. We went to listen to it in the forest of Soigne, as shortly afterwards we did for the thunder of the bombardment of Antwerp. From the wide ring boulevards near this shooting range where so many Belgians were to be shot, these incessant rumblings had the effect of a formidable storm. However, wasn't Antwerp the reputedly impregnable “national refuge”? we were soon to learn that in the proverbial struggle between breastplate and ball and chain, we were vastly inferior in 1914. But at the same time that people were beginning to fear for Antwerp, an unforeseen opportunity presented itself to escape the embrace. The professors from Louvain who had taken refuge in Brussels had just been summoned to the College S. Louis by their rector, Mgr. Lazy. It was explained to them that the University of Cambridge, moved by the destruction of our university, offered to transport our courses to its premises. Admittedly, the rector understood as we did the impossibility of responding completely to the wishes of our English friends, but their hospitable gesture could not meet with a refusal and we asked those of our teachers who could to find a way to win the England and to constitute there at least a university nucleus. Some colleagues obtained permission to travel by car to Holland via Maastricht. We decided to do the same. I went to the Commandantur to obtain the permit in question. I had to list my family members, including the governess. As one might fear that the latter was English, I insisted on the fact that she was indeed Belgian. To my great surprise, the employee immediately decreed that she could not obtain permission to cross the border. The Germans, however, could not ignore that they had authorized a number of Belgians to leave for Maastricht, but they only admitted the fiction that they were Dutch as long as these people did not expressly affirm their quality of Belgian subjects. We were therefore forced to give up this convenient means of leaving for Cambridge. Moreover, our colleague P. VAN DE VEN who wanted to accompany us hoped to find his wife in Ostend and insisted that we go to the sea. German requisitions. And forward! we hadn't yet left the built-up area when at the Anderlecht bridge the sentries blocked our way, demanding our driving license. For lack of anything better, I exhibited a small document that was given to milkmen in the suburbs, authorizing them to travel in a two-horse cart. But the note bore a stamp of the Commandantur! the latter had the usual magical effect on these soldiers. We could continue the road……… until new surprise. All went well as far as Hal and crossing a large herd of oxen on our way, we rejoiced to leave the country where, it seemed to us, the requisitions would soon lead to famine. Hal was occupied by troops of old classes. A pair of German officers, one tall and thin, the other round like a skin and both looking very out of place, made us think of Double Leg and Patachon. The very tired horses finally brought us to Enghien where, thanks to the kind burgomaster, we obtained a place in a hotel. The next day, we left this town very early in the morning, greeted at the exit by a picket of Austrian soldiers with a very inoffensive air, and we returned to a region still untouched by any contact with the enemy. You could even see Belgian postmen distributing letters to a population that knew very little of the serious events that seemed to affect most of the kingdom. In Ronse, crowds formed around our car. We were asked about the Germans and Brussels. We were advised to leave for Oudernade, which we did not fail to do despite the long hill where our weeds panted so much that we had to get out of the vehicle to lighten its weight. And now, to our great surprise, we discover that Audernade has just been occupied by German troops. A dashing officer shouts at us: “Warum flöhten Sie denn? » - « Wir flüchten gar nicht, we answer, wir reisen! » and in fact we are going towards a precise final goal. Despite our preoccupations, we admire the town hall which, in small form, reminded us so well of that of our poor Louvain. Our efforts to obtain more resistant horses remain unsuccessful and we decide to leave the nice little town. Unfortunately, at the exit of it, guards are waiting for us. You need a permit from the commander. My colleague and I walk back towards the main square, to the great fear of the ladies who see themselves already abandoned on this road. Arrived at the office in question, we have the good fortune to meet a consul of Portugal who was there with the same intentions as us. We understand that by forming a group with him, very willing to welcome us, we give ourselves the appearance of being protected by a country, then still neutral. In fact, the Germanic officer, all polished up in new-smelling leather, greeted us quite courteously. Wryly, however, he tells us that the war for him and his troops, very young reserves rushed west, was not only "fresh and joyful" but was a sporting race towards a slipping enemy. everywhere. The Yser was naturally soon going to undeceive him. In the meantime, he granted us permission to travel on the condition that we go towards Ghent, then occupied by their men. We are not long in joining the car and taking a completely different direction than Ghent without going too clearly towards the west. At nightfall, we are at Kruishoutem where our horses are collapsing. Impossible to stay in this village. Each on his own, runs to farms to ask to rent a horse. It was my wife who succeeded, not without having had to fend off the importunities of a drunken peasant. But that's just a kind of pony. No matter, its owner assures us that he will drag the heavy vehicle the heavy vehicle and at full speed, leaning hard to the side where the horse was attached to this drawbar made for two beasts, we set off into the night, along a narrow road lined with trees. Without incident, however, we reach Waregem, where the railway station is still in the hands of Belgian employees, but where the main square is covered with young peasants called up for military service. Only one hotel which is crowded. They did, however, take pity on my wife and my three children, and they made the servants of the inn rise to give us their beds. The next morning, the transport problem presents itself again. Not without difficulty, we discovered a small cart with a young horse and we left to soon encounter an English ambush waiting for the uhlans. The officer, very gentleman, examines our papers (so to speak) and with an elegant gesture, signals us to continue our journey. This is how we reach Roeselare where the whole population massed on the vast main square anxiously awaits the invasion. Near the station, a restaurant welcomes us. We find the Portuguese consul there. We order a good meal to recover from the emotions and fatigue of the day before. But suddenly, someone comes to announce that a train is going to leave for Lichtervelde. Is it worth taking it? Yes, assures the consul, because any step forward is welcome when one wants to escape the enemy, and sacrificing dinner, we carry as best we can the trunk containing all that remained of our possessions. We take the kids under the arm and pile into a wagon. In Lichtervelde, unfortunately, the convoy stops for good. Travelers rush to the village to obtain means of transport. It is who will arrive first and, at this decisive moment, our colleague realizes that he has forgotten the manuscript of a book to be published. We are forced to go and make declarations at the station and let the most diverse carts pass in front of us. In the end, we must be "all happy and easy" to rent a wheelbarrow to load the trunk and the baby. We would walk the road to Kortemark. In fiat, the weather is fine and the countryside engaging, to the point that some members of the group linger along the paths while, faithful to instructions, the peasant goes ahead with his wheelbarrow and his precious contents. I am out of breath following him and arrived at Kortemark station well before the others. There, after many talks, we get to take place in one of the ammunition trains used to evacuate the Belgian material from Ostend to the West. We are piled into a back van. A small stove is lit there, because the autumn is already cool and the coal which must feed the stove is scattered everywhere on the floor. There are other occupants in this obscure lair, among others a big bourgeoise to whom a French non-commissioned officer is courting fiercely and obviously is not far from achieving his ends. Certain beings are visibly incapable of allowing themselves to be penetrated by the tragedy of situations. Without fully understanding this one, children are a little more affected by it, because they deafen us with our cries. We need milk for the brat and as we stop at Zarren, my wife insists that I go and get some in the village or get a seat in the cars whose lights can be seen shining along the neighboring road. How to resist these instances? here I am in the small station, and… suddenly I see myself surrounded by very agitated Belgian officers. “Finally, we have one! " - " What do you want from me ? » - « You are one of those spies who infect the region! - "Absolute error, I was only asking where these cars are going and if they can't pick up my family?" - "Where is your family?" " - " In the train. » - « It's not his place in a military convoy and then… say! How do you explain your presence at ten o'clock in the evening on the passage of the troops to ask your questions there? » - « I am a professor from Louvain going by means of fortune to England where his rector sends him » - « Admit that you hardly look like what you say! » - « We are going to search you! - "What is this card?" » - « It's the one that authorizes me to go to my safe at Société Générale. » - « New implausibility! - However, nothing particularly suspicious is in my pockets and the officers move away, leaving me in the custody of a station employee. While I wonder what will happen to me, I question this man. " Where did they go ? » - « Look for the gendarmes! » - « But I cannot abandon my family! - "Why don't you join her?" » - « Because you are here! " - " Oh ! this is not an obstacle! » - « isn't there a sentry who would send me a gunshot? » - « No question of that! - Carefully, I slip in and see, alas! that the concoi has advanced. However, I see its red light in the distance and its speed does not exceed two per hour. A run along the track is in order. At a small bridge, I fall flat on my stomach because of two bars that are placed there to hold the rails. I feel injured in my legs and forehead, but time is running out and the race continues. I join the train where I find that my absence intrigues slightly but does not produce the concern that would be required. They forgot the instructions given and they believe me on a nearby car. Finally, around three o'clock in the morning, we arrive at Diksmuide. The atmosphere of the van has made me so thirsty that I try to refresh my lips with rainwater that is in the grooves of a barrier. We are allowed to sit in a railroad car dating from at least 1870 and try to sleep. In the dim light illuminating this gloomy bedroom, I can see that some of my traveling companions are smiling at the strange figure that I draw and I think, once again, that for many it is difficult to put themselves in the atmosphere that the times would impose. The next day, we see that Diksmuide is a real camp of the Belgian army. I have my little wound dressed while my wife goes from officer to officer to find out if her brother, then still under arms, is not there. Her research does not lead to the desired result but is not fruitless, as she discovers an officer who commanded the regiment in question. This ensures that this brother was evacuated to Dunkirk. This commando has, moreover, the kindness to load us in a car to reach Veurne. In this charming little town, the influx of soldiers is even greater than in Diksmuide. As I had previously stayed there at the “Noble Rose”, I bravely and naively led our group there and we placed the trunk heavily in the corridor, when a panicked servant ordered us to leave. “The King is here! A more modest inn allows us to take a little rest and think about the night that it will be impossible to spend in this city. At a street corner, all of a sudden, appears our driver whose mobilization had deprived us. However, it is not our car that he is driving. He tells us that the latter was thrown into the Scheldt when the Place d'Anvers was abandoned. We ask him to take us to La Panne, which he must decline, because he received orders excluding such a direction. We are forced to walk to this seaside resort where we hope to find accommodation. Luckily a military car took away women and children while my college and I continued the walk to La Panne. There, in fact, in a large hotel, now destroyed, they are willing to receive us. It's full of officers who naively laugh that my wife's bodice is torn. After a night spent in soiled sheets, the sun is shining under our windows and I go in search of a means of transport. We are assured, in fact, that La Panne is not safe, because a siege of Dunkirk is expected. Finding nothing, I suggest that my family take advantage of one of the large fishing boats stranded on the foreshore. This idea is very badly received. We are willing to endure everything on what has been called: "the bare ground", but to feel at the mercy of the capricious waves seems dreadful. Besides, my wife has no doubt that she will find another car. In fact, from 10 am, we are picked up by a car, but we have the unpleasant surprise to discover that it drops us off at Adinkerque. Here we are on the banks of the canal waiting for a new opportunity. A fairly long time passes until a car agrees to take away the women and children. My colleague and I are waiting in vain for such an advantage and are about to enter a barge which will take us pianissimo to the French port when, finally, a car agrees to collect us. And here is Dunkirk, on the threshold of which we are stopped and taken to French headquarters. Two French officers, not unpleasant but very talkative, end up accepting our vague identity documents and our affirmations and we go in search of the rest of the family who did not have any papers. We soon learned that a lady's smile and self-assurance were more than a passport, and that my wife had entered the fortress simply claiming that diplomats were following her. We find this audacious wife near the station, seated with our children around the table of a small cafe. Triumphantly she tells us that we will have this table available to spend the night. This perspective was unattractive, we decided to take a train to Calais earlier. Unfortunately, the number of amateurs is such in this city invaded by refugees that it is necessary to wait until the next day, just to obtain tickets. But don't we go to Cambridge in a commissioned service and can't we explain our case to the English consul? Immediately thought, immediately undertaken. My wife jumps into a taxi, unfortunately already occupied by a Belgian officer who gallantly gives way to us. The consul sends us to the admiralty which is established in the best hotel of the city: “the Red Hat”. We go there and even arrive in Calais to be admitted to the English admiral. In his language, we introduce ourselves as ex-Cambridge (which was my case) going to the Old varsity. We get to be able, the next day, to take place in a ship transporting the wounded to Dover. But the question of housing was not resolved. Seeing our success with the Admiralty, the innkeeper is willing to give up armchairs and a billiard table. We slept there, aided by fatigue, but disturbed by the proximity of a telephone which in the middle of the night was used to put the English commander on important operations in the navy, planned for the next day towards the Yser. The morning arrived, after a frantic race to the hospitals of Dunkirk to find my brother-in-law, we learned that the latter had been transported to England and my wife embarked from then on with all the more enthusiasm in the English boat. . The sea is good. The wounded Belgian officers don't seem too unhappy, even a little too good-natured in the eyes of those who from afar only see the war as heroes. Sitting on the bridge, there is no shortage of distractions because, at any moment, we come across English destroyers saluting us. They are the ones who go to the Yser to help stop the German advance on this little river which has since become famous. The arrival in Dover, at nightfall, put our patience to the test. Our boat must turn around to enter the port according to determined rules. From all sides in the night, the searchlights cast their rays. Finally, here we are on dry land and on a land that was then considered inviolable since aviation was only in its infancy and there was no talk of submarines yet. Once we are settled, finally, in a hotel, normal and in a country, which the war, we believed, could not reach, a joyful song escapes from our chests. Here ended, indeed, the somewhat "heroic" part of our exodus, the scope and duration of which were, however, to far exceed our conceptions at the time in question. Without incident, the next day we were to reach a London which did not seem to breathe an atmosphere of war and where we easily found accommodation for our group in a boarding house near Hyde Park. This was not yet the purpose of the trip, but we did not want to venture towards the small town of Cambridge without having made sure that accommodation was waiting for us there. Besides, we had to rebuild our wardrobe and wasn't London the perfect place to get dressed? My colleague and I scouted for Cambridge and found friends there who were unpleasantly surprised not to have seen us yet. Without hesitating any longer, we all left for this city where I had kept so good memories of my stay in 1901. Our faithful friend, Ernest Harrison of Trinity College, had reserved a nice little house for us near the vast "common", which is stretches across from the large Catholic Church of Our Lady and the English Martyrs. Although cramped, we could experience a very consoling “at home” feeling there after our adventures. The friendly welcome of our neighbors certainly contributed to this. Alone, my wife could not feel comfortable there until she had found her brother. Quite quickly, through the Belgian consulate, she managed to get in touch with him and got him to leave the military hospital to be treated with us. The young man suffered from a jaundice with haemorrhages which reigned in the trenches at the beginning of the war. By its contagious nature, it even communicated itself to one of our children. The presence of the newcomer made our little home more and more narrow and our friend Harrison obtained from his colleague at Trinty College, Professor Wothem, whose family was absent, that our household, joined to that of the colleague who had accompanied us in our wanderings can be established in the large villa owned by this “pretty well of” professor on Chaucer Road. This house, located on the Cam, upstream from the city, was very naturally called: Up Water Lodge. It was a charming place to stay surrounded by meadows and villas, a short distance from the admirable botanical garden of Cambridge where, in particular, the holm oaks which we no longer dare to plant at home, grow vigorously. Together with this appearance of home, we gave an appearance of a course in an appearance of a university. The latter had been organized in the premises of Emmanuel College, whose president, the linguist Giles had become an excellent friend since I had been his only pupil to follow his lessons in Indo-European syntax in 1901. The pupils were refugees, mainly Belgians, including quite diverse elements, even nuns. Our colleagues were, in particular, professors Dupriez, Van Gehuchten en Van den Ven from Louvain and coming from other universities: lrd professors L. de la Vallée-Poussin, Deschamps, etc. I gave lessons there in Old French, and I often spent my mornings in the old library adjoining the Senate House where, as a student in 1901, I had liked to browse - as was then permitted - in all the departments. , in order to prepare a study on the Indian god: Yama. I was happy to see my work once again punctuated by the silvery tones of the carillon on St Mary the Great, so typical of Cxambridge like, moreover, the low sounds of the organs of the glorious Kings College Chapel where, as an English poet says , “music dwells, as loath to die”. But little by little these comforts felt threatened by the departure of almost all the students, called to the front and by the disappearance of certain professors. One of the missing, alas! was the great neurologist Van Gehuchten, who died suddenly in a Cambridge clinic after being operated on for appendicitis. This man, still young and of a gay character, had, a few days before entering the hospital, talked pleasantly with us at Up Water Lodge. His burial attracted those of our colleagues who had taken refuge in Oxford to Cambridge, and Professor Denys, very affected by his death, delivered the funeral eulogy of this learned man in the cemetery, whose son continues today the career so prematurely interrupted. The departure of Professor Dupriez had, on the contrary, had no tragic character. He had been called to the other Cambridge, that of Massachusetts, where, having just landed, he was taken to an auditorium to give an inaugural course. As the so-called "Belgian University of Cambridge" was visibly crumbling, I tried to obtain a more lasting appointment in the United States as well. I had once been the almost unique pupil of Professor Waldenstein, who taught the history of Greek art in the nice museum of ancient sculptures at the University of Cambridge. This character was a neutralized Romanian Jew who had transformed himself into an English lord and owned an imposing castle in the countryside. His relations with his fellow Americans were important and I did not hesitate to approach him to obtain an invitation to an overseas university. It came to me suddenly, sooner than I wanted. A telegram gave me a very early date to present myself at Columbia University in New York. As my wife was about to give me a fourth child, I would have preferred to postpone this trip, but I was made to understand that it would be completely losing the opportunity that presented itself. Entrusting therefore the fate of my wife to an excellent doctor and, in spite of the disappointment that I gave to my English friends who were not very admiring of the Americans, but also not very foreseeing of the duration of the war, I left for London in order to take the bodt train to Liverpool. The latter was stuffed with Americans whose noisy animation was, in fact, a flagrant contrast with the phlegm of England. In Liverpool, a Belgian was responsible for ascertaining the nationality of those who embarked by presenting himself as his compatriots. He asked me to say a few sentences in Flemish and was quickly edified. The crossing of the American Line was done without incident Charming at the beginning under the influence of the currents of the Azores, it became difficult around Newfoundland where the traditional "blissart" of the beginning of April was already blowing, which was still raging in our arrival in New York. I spent a lot of time in the steamer saloon to urgently prepare five or six introductory lessons on various subjects, since I remembered the adventure of my colleague Dupriez and I had absolutely no idea what I would be made to teach at Columbia. On arrival in the large port, the Statue of Liberty took on a very special significance for the one fleeing occupied Belgium, but this monument seemed to me too small in the immensity of the spectacle. This one was mainly frightening by the apocalyptic view of Manhattan with its skyscrapers of all shapes, erected in a prodigious block, one after the other and among which there was even one in Gothic style. One of my traveling companions seeing my astonishment whispered in my ear that all this was only the reign of money and the thirst for wealth and did not deserve the admiration of a European intellectual. He was certainly not entirely wrong, but he ignored many qualities that materialistic preoccupations do not stifle in the Americans, qualities which were displayed to the maximum in the way in which they then received Belgians, because the fate of those this had affected them deeply. The welcome was quite different from that received by my friend, Dupriez. Two very courteous friends of Waldstein received me at the wharf and took me to Columbia where I learned that I was given 15 days to prepare lessons, on the one hand on Iranian languages and on the other on the comparative grammar of novel. While waiting to begin these courses, I was asked to help a pupil of the Iranianist Jackson to translate the episode of Sevitrf in the Mahabharata. So I immediately became a bookworm, at a time when, by buying Bethleem Steel, I could have made almost a fortune. One day, leaving the library at Columbia, I had the impression of being attacked by a high fever. Entering this building in the morning shivering, I suddenly found myself in a bath of 35 degrees. Such are, in fact, the temperature swings in the American spring, subject alternately to the winds from Baffin's Sea or those from the West Indies, creating what are called there cold or hot spells. This heat was not long in transforming the surroundings of New York into verdant hills where the flowers of an early dogwood with large bracts of white snow could be seen from afar. The undergrowth, more completely parched by frost than at home, began to fill with the ample leaves of the skonk cabbage (a kind of arum) and we felt drawn towards the brushwood that we saw on the banks of facing that mighty Hudson River, flowing down from the heights where Columbia University lay gracefully. But I didn't just venture around New York. I was going to Philadelphia, where certain people lived who had made the crossing with me and had assured me that I would find a warm welcome at the University of Pennsylvania. Visiting the rector of this institution, I had the pleasant surprise to learn, in fact, that they were thinking of approving a Belgian professor and that the orientalist Jastrow - a fellow Waldsteiner - had heard of my presence. at Columbia and insisted that I be offered a chair in general linguistics and Greek. It goes without saying that this offer was timely, because at Columbia I was only invited for three months. So when, continuing my little journey, I went to the Catholic University of Washington, I had to decline the offer of a chair in Orientalism, remunerated, moreover, much less generously than in Philadelphia. The proposal had been made to me by the well-known orientalist, Hyvernat, who had imagined that I was an ecclesiastic because of my type of specialty. This excellent colleague nevertheless remained one of our best friends and a frequent visitor during our stay in the United States. Obtaining a fixed position and a regular income made it possible for my family, who remained on English soil, to come to America. On the other hand, the conversations I had in New York, especially with the French professor Pradelle made me understand that the war by submarines would only increase and therefore, I decided to send to Up Water Lodge a telegram sufficiently alarming to persuade my people to cross the sea without further delay. The text of this message intrigued, however, the English security who came in vain to inquire from my people about the type of special information we had. In the meantime, the birth of little Ethel had taken place and the baby was already fit to be transported. So I learned one day, with pleasure, that I should tend to see a group of fourteen people arrive. It was a sweltering day in July when five hundred horses had died of heat. We saw their corpses in the streets and this hot spell had caused quite a few victims in the population, already devastated by an epidemic of infantile paralysis which had penetrated even among the listeners of my courses. A legend, reproduced later by the Pourquoi Pas de Bruxelles was created, no one knows how. She says that despite the extreme heat, I had prepared big overcoats for the arrivals. In fact, I had prepared for everyone only temporary lodgings in New York until we settled in Philadelphia. However, colleagues from the University of Pennsylvania were, without delay, kind enough to allow the family to be housed for a few days in a dormitory (we would say in Louvain: a "pedagogy") then deserted by the students in time vacation and very soon after a house on Chester Avenue was able to receive us, while my colleague's family was going to settle in Princeton. We had the annoyance of noticing soon that our two servants recruited in England and whose passage had been paid for left us without any other form of trial, undoubtedly attracted by the American wages which were however then very low in comparison with the current era. We paid, in fact, the replacements eight dollars a month. Several of them were negresses, among whom there were some who disappeared with various objects. So we were very grateful to the friends who provided us with a French woman from La Ferté Milon, who remained very attached to us. In fact, we could not be too grateful for so many people who opened their doors in this Philadelphia where the old families (those with at least three generations in the oldest cemetery in the city) nevertheless constitute a rather closed world, like Europeans do not expect to find in the United States, but which nevertheless exists not only in Philadelphia, where people like to descend from the Quakers of William Penn, but also in Boston, where they must have had an ancestor on the May Flower, the ship that brought the "first pelgrims" to New England. It was also thanks to these interesting connections that we obtained the means of escaping the humid and oppressive heat of the Philadelphian summers, by settling in a large villa at Drifton in the Alleghanies. The reception given to the “research professor” at the university was no less cordial. Professors Jastrow, Edgerton, Kent, Crosby, Crawford, Taggart, Hyde and many others have acquired a very lasting claim to our recognition. The Classical Philology Seminary was an ideal place to compose the numerous articles, destined for American journals after having been used for small conferences in the meetings of scientific societies, quite active in the United States and where it was expected that the foreign professor brought something new. It was there, too, that our study of the mythology of Iran was completed, prepared at the request of the linguist RL GRAY in the rich library of Columbia University and which was to be illustrated by the reproduction of miniatures borrowed from the Persian manuscripts of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Not only these congress meetings, but the delicious intellectual evenings of the Franklin Club gave the opportunity to make or hear interesting communications. Let us add that in Philadelphia, as in most American universities, receptions between colleagues were frequent and full of charming intimacy. For her part, my wife was invited to lecture in society circles on Belgium and its literature. We met the members of these same circles at the Little Theater where French plays were given. My wife's main occupation was, however, her participation in the Belgian Relief organized in Philadelphia by a circle of ladies, among whom were Mmes Bayard-Henry, Cawalader, Coxe, etc. This collaboration notably included conferences in various settings. Besides my wife, my sister-in-law Susanne Silvercruys excelled in this kind of activity. In her twenties, after having learned English in a boarding school in Georgetown (Washington DC), she proved to be an excellent speaker and had great success in many towns under the name of Little Belgian Girl. Alongside my scientific work, I myself was taken to this kind of propaganda whose usefulness was to intensify in intellectual circles the climate favorable to the allies and to Belgium. I even founded with my colleague P. Van de Ven a Belgian Bureau of Information next to our embassy in Washington, which was then worthily chaired by Baron Cartier de Marchienne. The aim was to concentrate information on Belgium and distribute it in the form of articles in American newspapers. To this pen work was added that of the conferences. One of these was given to a businessmen's club in Philadelphia: the Clover Club. It even served - in a very American way - as a starting point in the newspapers for certain advertisements. On the other hand, while she was giving herself, my wife, without my knowledge, was taken to a clinic in Germantown (near Philadelphia) where she was to give birth to our son, Georges. I went in and fell asleep, unaware of this fact and was very surprised to be woken up by the telephone around five o'clock in the morning to learn of this birth. Hardly understanding this unexpected message, I received it rather badly, for I feared that it was a bad joke from some adorer of my sister-in-law, Susanne. Another comic incident occurred during the presidential election. Hughes, Wilson's competitor was one of the few Americans to wear a beard. Now the first results gave the majority to this one and provoked in the main street of Philadelphia a noisy enthusiasm among the crowd with which I was mingled. The latter, seeing in me almost a double of Hughes, carried me in triumph. What rested a little from this hectic and more than active life were the summer stays at the Coxes' estate in Drifton. Although we were in the middle of mining country, the landscapes had their charm. On the one hand there were the Pennsylvania Dutch valleys, occupied by the descendants of the Württemberg veterans of the war of independence and which completely recalled Swabia, on the other hand the vast wooded hills of the Alleghanies whose foliage veiled the slag heaps and surface coal mining. It is a wonderful opportunity to become acquainted with American nature. Already, in Philadelphia, I had joined the naturalist excursions of Professor Mac-Farlane, who knew the flora of Pennsylvania and New Jersey thoroughly, and especially those of the beautiful valleys of Wissahikon Park. But the vast forests of the Alleghanies were even more interesting. Along with their numerous kinds of oaks, they still possessed the chestnut trees which were soon to be suppressed by the implacable disease which extirpated them from Pennsylvania. The undergrowth abounded in blueberries of all and was adorned with laurels (Kalmia) with graceful pink flowers. There were unfortunately also rattlesnakes there, whose sinister noise was sometimes heard even near our villa. Less disturbing, but much noisier was the music of our cicadas and grasshoppers which, during the hot nights, resounded incessantly in all tones. It is the same with those insects which imitated the songs of birds. On the other hand there were the birdies, the humming birds which foraged on the flowers like the twilight sphinxes and the entomological glory of America, were the large ledidoptera relatives of our swallowtails but displaying more varied colors and more gleaming, while a large moth swung its broad, pale green wings heavily. Autumn (indian fall) set the whole landscape ablaze with the ruddy hues of the maples, liquidambars, dogwoods, sumacs, etc., as well as the gold of the tulip trees and the burning brown of the oaks. We were beginning to love this Pennsylvania despite the too many and too extreme variations in its climate and the multiple thaws, so often turning Philadelphia into a cesspool. But the temptation to find more lenient skies and to penetrate into the romantic Far-West worked in us and contributed to our accepting the offer of a professorship in linguistics at the University of California, located at Berkeley near San Francisco. It was on a particularly icy winter evening, during the session of one of those congresses which essentially serve to recruit professors, that in New Haven (Conn.), Professor Schevill decided to escape these frosts and leave for the Pacific coast. It was not without regret that we left our nice house on Spruce Street and our many friends in Philadelphia both in the “world” and at the University. I entrusted to other hands the office in Washington where my brother-in-law, after having been a professor at the University of Michigan, had received a post as embassy attaché. He took in my sister-in-law, who couldn't leave the East where her role as lecturer was so precious. It was also in Washington that President Wheeler of Berkeley worked out the details of our departure and establishment at his university. As in New York, I had to go ahead of my family again this time, because I had to participate in a Summer Session, before starting the actual classes. While my people were still establishing themselves this season, in Drifton, I therefore left for the west via Buffalo, where I was able to contemplate Niagara Falls under the dim light of an eclipse of the sun (I had seen them two years ago). , before, in the middle of winter, surrounded by large heaps of ice, worthy of the polar regions. The great horizons of Arizona left an unforgettable impression on me, as well as the Great Canyon, one of the great wonders of this world, the colored desert and the plains near Mexico where yuccas, cacti and dracaenas spread their twisted arms and bizarre snowshoes Curious also the banks of the Rio Grande where Indian tribes still continue their traditional existence with their little horses, their tents and their colorful costumes Los Angeles, which was then only a quarter of what it has since become, did not particularly impress me, but San Francisco presented me with one of the most beautiful landscapes in the world. the atmosphere there seems too cold to one who comes from the eastern summer. Gradually, you get used to this temperature, which stays around 17 to 18 degrees all year round. This famous climate of California certainly deserves the reputation it has been given as well as the admiration of the inhabitants. It is, indeed, proverbial that every Californian asks every visitor: “what do you think of our climate? ". as in Philadelphia, we inquire about the number of ancestors, in Boston about what we know, in New York about what we have, in Chicago about what we know how to do, and so on. It is on this coast, a real riviera, differing from that of Nice by its light mists and by the freshness of its summer, but very similar to it by its vegetation, because however paradoxical it may be, we find at this distance from the Mediterranean laurels, venerable holm oaks and capricious pines. The drought is greater in California than in Brovence. For six months, not a drop of water fell and the gray hills were covered with succulent and aromatic plants that tolerated the drought. Only the valleys are shaded by oak oaks with dark foliage. The dryness of the soil is suitable for a kind of burrowing squirrels which swarm in places more than the rabbits here. The University, whose white buildings and the graceful campanile can be seen from afar, has, however, been able to surround itself with a more cheerful setting thanks to vast plantations of eucalyptus, palm trees, mimosas and above all operating artificially the afforestation of the heights which overhang it. The view enjoyed from these hills and the Golden Gate is prestigious, especially at sunset, when the last lights of these still gild the summit of Mount Tamalpais which plays in this whole landscape the role of Vesuvius in the bay of Naples. The birdsong is missing. No other sound than the monotonous notes of a gentle sparrow and the heavy rustling of blue jays. The University, one of the most important in the United States, has admirable facilities and offers, in particular to its professors, a graceful Faculty Club where I found refuge during the first months of my stay and where one can maintain very pleasant conversations. Between the Summer Session and the opening of classes, however, I hastened to leave these charming places to explore the superb surrounding region. The nearest and most indicated excursion leads to the Muiy Woods where, in a large fold of ground, spreads a forest of gigantic specimens of these "Red Woods" (Sequoia sempervirens) whose very resistant pink wood is unfortunately appreciated to the point of having led to the felling of too many of these enormous Palos Altos, as the Spaniards say, but the Muir Woods have escaped and under their imposing shades there is vegetation which seems to have wanted to be in tune with the forest, because even the exalids there are three times the size of ours. From these wonderful woods, we undertake the ascent of Mount Tamalpais from where we dominate the whole region on a clear day but from where, that evening, my friend Woodbridge and I were blessed with an immense sea of clouds. As imposing as the Muir Woods are; they cannot be compared to Sequia National Park, near Fresno, where I always went. This is the botanical brother of the sequoia sempervirens, the sequoia giganta which still exceeds it in size and longevity. Fifteen hundred of these giants (1,000 to 2,000 years old) adorn this forest, unique in the world, which I traveled in all directions without worrying about the heavy fall of the formidable pine cones (pinus Lambertiam), nor the lion-pumas, the grizzly bears and coyote wolves that inhabit these woods and whose various cries disturbed the silence of my nights spent in a cabin at the foot of a tree more than thirty meters in circumference. Less imposing, but hardly less interesting, is the region of Lake Tshoe which I traveled with some of my colleagues. There is a mountain hotel on the shores of the small lake called Fallen Leaf, because its shape is reminiscent of an oak leaf fallen on the ground. It is an admirable center for excursions, comprising small ascents towards the Desolation Valley, with bare rocks contrasting with the varied vegetation of these valleys where pines and lobocedrons dominate above all. The fauna includes beavers, as well as chipmunks, friendly little squirrels, not very shy to the point of coming to share our pick-nicks in wild places where they certainly had not been able to familiarize themselves with humans. Despite the charms of these excursions, I longed to see my friends again, who lingered beyond measure, not remembering the pleasures of a stay in the Alleghanys. They were, moreover, waiting for clarification as to the dwelling which awaited them in the distant West. In fact, it was only after much effort that I found a villa large enough to accommodate them. It was, it is true, very spacious and admirably encamped on the hills of North Berkley, where the numerous villas of the professors rose in tiers. It fully deserved its name of Buena Vista by the panorama it offered towards the bay and the Golden Gate, this golden door where the extreme west of European civilization, which we had finally reached, opens a road towards the Far East across the vastness of the Pacific Ocean. My wife was quickly charmed by this decor, by the table laden with beautiful fruits that California produces in abundance, as well as by the balconies where, in the open air, the family could sleep. Our neighbors were, moreover, very agreeable though sometimes strange, since Berkeley attracts not only scholars but artists and eccentrics of various genres. Next to us stood a kind of Greek temple where the family of a friend and follower of Isidoria Duncan spent their life in the middle of nature, eating nuts and performing dances in the mountains in the cool of the mornings. This dream landscape led, moreover, my wife to imitate it with her granddaughters. This sunny existence was darkened by the terrible epidemic of the "Spanish flu" which reached this heavenly land like the whole world at the end of the war. Special precautions were, however, taken and the wearing of a tulle mask was made strictly compulsory, which curbed the contagion. This one had nevertheless done a lot

description: Transcription in "Croix Rouge Suisse Pro Captivis" notebook for the German prisoners of war. Below is the transcription in fair copy (with additions for better understanding) by Gert Schmidt (son). War diary 1915 – 1920 by Erich Schmidt * December 21, 1896. Italics = subsequent additions for better understanding by Gert Schmidt, otherwise reproduced verbatim. 1915 05.10. position command received. 06.10. Journey home (to Cottbus). 07.10. drove back to Berlin. 08.10. Position in Schöneberg (Berlin). Departure from Tempelhof (Berlin). First meal in Kreutg in the evening... illegible. ? 09.10. Morning in Stargard (Pomeranian). 10.10. Arrival in Königsberg (East Prussia) at night. 12.10. first service. 27.10. Swearing-in ceremony in the Castle Church. 06.11. Departure to Memel. (East Prussia) 07.11. Arrival in Memel. 14.11. The first lice. 24.12. first watch. 07.11.1915 to 08.07.1916 probably stationed in Memel. 1916 06.05. First vacation of 5 days 08.07. Assignment for transport in the morning, departure at 2 o'clock in the afternoon. Evening in Tilsit (East Prussia). 09.07. In the morning in Königsberg, in the evening in Marienburg (East Prussia). 10.07. In the morning in Schneidemühl (Pomerania), in the afternoon in Berlin. 11.07. At noon in Kassel, in the evenings in Bad Ems, Koblenz, Cobern on the Moselle. 12.07. Morning in Diedenhofen (Lorraine, then German). Drive across the French border at Audun-le-Roman - Longuagon - Landres - Audun-le-Roman. Unloaded and onward march to Serrouville. 07/15 Last bath on German soil at Böllingen colliery in Lorraine. 07/17 March to Nouillon-Pout. There service as honorary company. 21.07. Meeting the Crown Prince. 23.07 Illness to march through. 07/29 Departure from Nouillon-Pout via Longuagon - Montmedy - Sedan to Sun-sur-Marne. Rest and march on via Billig and Lion. 07/30 March to Vilosnes-sur-Marne. 06.08. March to the "Dead Man". 08/13 Detachment and return to Vilosnes-sur-Marne. 08/15 March to Ville forest camp via Sifry and Lamvillers. 08/17 March to Thiaumont via Wavrillenwald - Foss-sur-Gorge - Chambrettferine - Totenschlucht escarpment and Thiaumont Gorge. Before Verdun, 70,000 soldiers from both armies were killed in fighting between French and German troops. 08/18 Captured (lucky despite everything that followed) and marched off to Verdun. 08/18 Arrival at the penal camp. 01.09. Departure to Dombasle. (Name of a camp in Lorraine. Stay probably from the beginning of September to the end of December 1916). 20.12. Determination of the (groin) hernia. 1917 01.01. Departure for Vadelaincourt. taken bath. 02.01. Departure for Pioneer Park Vadelaincourt. 07.01 First post. 08.01. Departure to the penal camp. 10.01. Frozen left foot. 01/11 Departure from Souilly via Troyes. 01/13 Arrival in Orleans. 01/14 Departure for Bruay via Amiens. 01/16 Arrival in Bruay. size 191/I. title: Gravfält
description:
Gravfält, delvis undersökt, ca 150 x 50-70 m (NV-SÖ). Inom angivet område har M Strömberg under åren 1951, 1957, 1962 samt 1971-1973 undersökt ca 130 gravar. Före undersökningen kunde 4 låga överodlade högar, 14-22 m diam iakttas. Ursprungligt antal gravar på platsen uppskattas i rapporten till ca 175 st. Datering av gravarna: Mellanneolitisk stridsyxekultur - sen romerskjärnålder. Mellanneolitikum, 3 skelettgravar. Fynd av bl.a. pärlor, kopparspiral, håleggad yxa. Senneolitikum och äldre bronsålder, ett 40-tal gravar, bl.a. 8 stenkistor. Fynd av bl.a. diverse flintartefakter, enstaka bronser. Bronsålder - äldre järnålder, ett 80-tal brandgravar. Fynd av bl.a.diverse bronsföremål, lerkärl. Järnålder, 4 skelettgravar. Fynd av bl.a. järnkniv, pärlor, bronser. - Vid revideringsinventeringen 1987 kunde platsen ej besiktigas på grund av gröda.  - - 
Tillägg dnr 321-3083-2004: Regionmuseet Kristianstad utförde en arkeologisk förundersökning (schaktövervakning) 2003, S om gravfältet. Ett 300 m l, 0,6 m br och 1,2 m dj schakt grävdes parallellt samt ca 9 m N om en bilväg. NÖ om gravfältet framkom 1 urnegrav och 1 härd.  Graven bestod av en nedgrävning, ca 0,4 m diam och 0,5 m dj. I botten påträffades en 2 urnor med br ben, placerade ovanpå varandra. Benen från urnorna antagligen härrör från samma individ. Graven daterades till förromersk järnålder möjligen y bronsålder. Härden var 1,6 m l och 0,24 m dj. Avståndet mellan lämningarna var ca 0,5 m. - - 
Tillägg dnr 321-4143-2006: År 2006 utfördes en arkeologisk förundersökning SÖ om gravfältet med anledning av grävning för optokabel. Ett ca 5 m långt schakt i vägkanten besiktigades. Under ca 0,75 m påförda massor (vägbank) vidtog ett ca 0,2 m tjockt matjordslager. Under matjorden kom steril sand. Det bedömdes som problemfritt att lägga kabeln i den sedan länge påförda vägbanken,

title: Lushögen, High
description:
High, residue of, partially investigated, about 20x12 m (N-S) and next to 1m h. Growth with a variety of pines planted. The mound was partially examined in 1918 by Simrishamn’s museum. The mound found inter alia a stone casket (no finds?), an urn (Roman skitty), and a stone gasket, about 1 m pcs, m fragments of 2 bronze strings. E Lönnberg (1933) refers to the fact that amber pearls were found in the mound, but that they were broken. Appendix dnr 321-3083-2004: The Region Museum Kristianstad carried out an archaeological investigation (shaft control) in 2003, S-om högen. An approximately 80 m l and 1 m br scakt were excavated. No antiquarian interest emerged.
